newsitem.title: FRANCE: Netanyahu says Arafat must calm tensions.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says Arafat must calm tensions.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said during a European tour overshadowed by Israeli-Palestinian violence that Yasser Arafat must try to calm tensions for the sake of peace.

On the worst day of bloodshed in the West Bank since he took office in June, an exuberant Netanyahu revelled in the applause of French Jewish supporters of his right-wing Likud party on Wednesday as he spelled out his election theme of "peace with security".

Referring only briefly to Wednesday's violence -- in which Israeli troops on the edge of PLO-ruled Ramallah opened fire on stone-throwing Palestinians, killing seven and wounding more than 300 -- he told the crowd of 4,500 at the Paris rally:
"Whoever is in a position of leadership...should calm passions and not inflame them. He should return to the negotiating table and not preach violence."
Although the Israeli leader did not mention Arafat by name, the reference was clear.

Earlier a senior Israeli official accompanying Netanyahu on a tour of Britain, France and Germany charged the Palestinian president was behind the violence sparked by Israel's opening of a tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem near Islam's third-holiest shrine.
The bloodshed poured fuel on Palestinians' fury over what they view as Netanyahu's foot-dragging on implementing peace moves agreed upon by his predecessor Shimon Peres.

Netanyahu had already been roundly criticised throughout the Arab world for rejecting the formula of trading occupied land for peace, a U.S.-endorsed principle that had driven peace talks forward under Peres's Labour.
"This government is trying to undermine the very foundations of the peace process," said Palestinian minister Hanan Ashrawi.
Arafat said the violence had thrown relations with the Netanyahu government into crisis. He condemned the opening of the tunnel as a "crime" and an attempt to "judaise" the city.
The French foreign ministry said the tunnel opening "adds a new and regrettable factor of tension."
Netanyahu, in a rousing rally speech, invoked the spirit pf assassinated Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, saying Sadat's pledge of "no more war" had been unconditional.

"I tell you we have to return to this basic standard, and stop the (Arab) threats, violence, terror, war -- to halt the threatening rhetoric which says we are harming the Moslem holy places. This is untrue."
Netanyahu appeared at the rally after holding telephone consultations with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

Earlier he held talks with French President Jacques Chirac and told reporters the latest violence would probably delay a planned negotiating session with Arafat's Palestinian Authority from Thursday until Sunday.

Netanyahu said after meeting Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe that he believed "France through its good relations with Arab countries could help Israel in its search for peace...and we are open to this cooperation."
Netanyahu flies to Germany on Thursday. He will visit the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp before holding talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
An Israeli official said Netanyahu would raise with Kohl the danger of Iraq or Iran acquiring nuclear weapons.
